text: Parastou Forouhar (Persian; پرستو فروهر), born in 1962 in Tehran, Iran, is an Iranian installation artist who lives and works in Frankfurt, Germany. She is the daughter of political activist Parvaneh Forouhar (née Eskandari) and politician Dariush Forouhar, whose opposition to the Iranian government led him to found and lead the Hezb-e-Mellat-e Iran (Nation Party of Iran), a far-right secular opposition party. Her parents were stabbed to death in their home on November 22, 1998, in a secret operation carried out by the Iranian Intelligence service, an event widely known as the Chain Murder. This tragedy has deeply influenced her artistic practice, which serves as a critical response to the politics of Iran and Islamic fundamentalism, and challenges viewers to confront war crimes against innocent citizens. Despite the incident occurring over 35 years ago, the Iranian state intelligence continues to obstruct public commemoration of her parents and has threatened her multiple times; she was ultimately sentenced to six years of conditional prison in 2017. Forouhar studied art at the University of Tehran from 1984 to 1990, earning her B.A., and later pursued her M.A. at the Hochschule für Gestaltung in Offenbach am Main, Germany, completing it in 1994. She now lives in Frankfurt, Germany, with her two children. Her work is autobiographical and engages with the political and cultural dynamics shaping contemporary Iranian citizenship both in Iran and abroad. She works across various media, including site-specific installation, animation, digital drawing, photography, signs, and products, using culturally specific motifs such as Islamic calligraphy and Persian miniature painting to question the constraints of standardized beauty and cultural identity. Her artworks initially appear poetic and aesthetically pleasing, with smooth lines and vivid colors, but upon closer inspection reveal hidden realities of state violence and oppression. One of her notable works, Kahrizak Prison, references the 2009 incident in which Green Movement protesters were tortured and raped at the Kahrizak detention center, resulting in at least five deaths; the butterfly motif, referencing her mother Parvaneh’s name, symbolizes both her personal loss and the broader suffering of oppressed populations, evoking the imagery of murdered butterflies in a collection. In 2002, the Iranian Cultural Ministry censored her photo exhibition Blind Spot, which featured a veiled, gender-neutral figure with a featureless face; in response, Forouhar displayed only the empty frames on opening night. In 2012, she received the Sophie von La Roche Award for her work addressing displacement, gender, and cultural identity. Solo exhibitions of her work have taken place at Stavanger Cultural Center, Norway; Golestan Art Gallery, Tehran; Hamburger Bahnhof – Museum fur Gegenwart, Berlin; City Museum, Crailsheim, Germany; and German Cathedral, Berlin. She has also participated in group exhibitions at Framer Framed, Amsterdam; Schim Kunsthalle, Frankfurt; Frauenmuseum Bonn; Museum of Modern Art, Frankfurt; Neue Galerie am Landesmuseum, Joanneum, Graz, Austria; House of World Cultures, Berlin; Deutsches Hygiene-Museum, Dresden; Jewish Museum of Australia, Melbourne; Law Warschaw Gallery at Macalester College, Saint Paul; and Jewish Museum San Francisco. Her work is held in permanent collections at the Queensland Art Museum, Queensland; Belvedere, Vienna; Badisches Landesmuseum, Karlsruhe; Museum of Modern Art, Frankfurt; and the Deutsche Bank Art Collection. Forouhar has been featured in art fairs such as the Brodsky Center Fair at Rutgers University in 2015 and the Pi Artworks fair in Istanbul and London in 2016 and 2017, attending both locations.
